problems.memo_sentence: The authors note that their analysis and demonstrations are restricted to univariate distributions, explicitly acknowledging that multivariate cases lie beyond the present scope.
problems.source_evidence: "Our analyses focused on univariate distributions, but can be extended to multivariate forms."
problems.explanation: The memo states the restriction as a limitation, but the paper frames multivariate cases as an extension rather than a hard scope limitation. This changes the meaning from a present constraint to a future possibility.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors also state that the continuous-distribution circuit based on their unitary gate set cannot directly prepare general discrete probability distributions except in the trivial single-qubit case, requiring an auxiliary complementary-state construction for the discrete setting.
problems.source_evidence: "It is not possible to prepare (28) from the set of unitary gate operations depicted in Fig. 2, except when n = 1."
problems.explanation: The memo captures the need for an auxiliary construction, but it omits the paper's explicit limitation that the Fig. 2 unitary-gate circuit cannot prepare the discrete state for n>1. That limitation is central to the paper's discrete-case discussion.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors adapt a classical upsampling technique from FFT-based time-series analysis to design a divide-and-conquer quantum state-preparation algorithm built from controlled Y-rotation gates, where rotation angles are defined from ratios of probabilities.
problems.source_evidence: "we apply an upsampling method of data capture, most often associated with classical fast Fourier transform analysis of discrete samples of time series, to the construction of a quantum algorithm" and "The quantum circuit ... is transformable to an equivalent circuit of polylogarithmic gate depth [10] using a method of quantum forking [11]."
problems.explanation: The upsampling adaptation is the paper's own contribution, but the polylogarithmic-depth transformation via quantum forking is explicitly attributed to Araujo et al. [10] and Park et al. [11]. The memo presents that part as if it were developed by the authors of this paper.
